Before you buy

These short guides cover what to check before you apply:

  • The hidden costs of final expense insurance: underwriting classes, waiting periods and the premium math.
  • What final expense costs at 65, 70 and 75: what sets the price.

  • How much a funeral costs, and who pays: your rights when you shop, and who pays when there is no policy.

Veterans: If the person was a veteran, VA may pay an allowance toward part of the burial, funeral, and plot or interment costs. replacements.old:
Can I qualify with health problems?
Almost always yes. Most final expense plans are simplified-issue — no medical exam, just a few health questions — and many carriers approve common conditions like diabetes and heart disease. If your health is more serious, guaranteed-issue options exist that accept you regardless of health history.
Will my premium ever go up?
No. Final expense is whole life insurance, so your premium is locked in the day your policy starts and never increases — no matter your age or any changes in your health.
How much coverage do I need?
Many people choose an amount close to the funeral and final bills they expect to leave. We'll help you decide the right amount for your situation without overselling you.
How fast does my family get the money?
Usually within days of filing a claim. The death benefit is paid directly to your beneficiaries, tax-free, so they have cash on hand quickly to handle funeral and final expenses.
replacements.new:
Can I qualify with health problems?
Often, yes. Many final expense plans ask a few health questions instead of a medical exam, and some insurers accept common conditions like diabetes and heart disease. Each insurer sets its own rules. If your health is more serious, guaranteed-issue plans skip the health questions, but they have a waiting period. If death happens in the first years of the policy, often the first 2 or 3, the policy may pay only a reduced amount, such as the premiums paid, instead of the full benefit. Graded-benefit plans also pay less in the early years. The exact terms are in the policy, so read them before you buy. See how a graded death benefit works.
Will my premium ever go up?
Usually not. A whole life final expense policy normally sets the premium when the policy starts and keeps it level for as long as you pay it. Check the premium terms in the policy before you buy to confirm yours works that way.
How much coverage do I need?
Many people choose an amount close to the funeral and final bills they expect to leave. We'll help you decide the right amount for your situation without overselling you.
How fast does my family get the money?
The insurer pays after it receives proof of death, such as a certified copy of the death certificate, and the completed claim forms. How long that takes depends on the insurer and the claim. The money goes directly to the beneficiaries you name. Under IRS rules, proceeds paid because of the insured person's death are generally not taxable income, but interest paid on them is.

replacements.old: Final expense whole life is a genuinely useful product. It can be the right answer for many families — especially those who want simple, permanent coverage for funeral and burial costs without medical exams or complex underwriting. But it's also one of the most aggressively marketed products in the senior insurance market, and the wrong policy can cost you thousands in extra premium over the years it's in force.
replacements.new: Final expense whole life can be a useful product. It can be the right answer for many families, especially those who want simple, permanent coverage for funeral and burial costs without a medical exam. But it is heavily marketed to seniors, and the wrong policy can mean paying more premium than you need to for as long as you keep it.
replacements.why: Removes the superlative "one of the most aggressively marketed products" and the unsourced dollar claim "cost you thousands".

replacements.old:
The argument for final expense is straightforward: average funeral costs in the United States now run several thousand dollars and often into five figures. Many families don't have that liquid. When death comes unexpectedly, the cost falls on grieving spouses and adult children, often paid through credit cards, hardship withdrawals from retirement accounts, or quick-sold belongings.

A small, permanent whole life policy — usually $10,000 to $25,000 in face amount — solves this. Premiums never change. Once issued, the coverage doesn't expire. The death benefit pays out tax-free, typically within a couple of weeks of a filed claim. That's real value.
replacements.new:
The argument for final expense is straightforward: a funeral is a large bill, and it often comes with little warning. The National Funeral Directors Association publishes national median funeral prices from its 2023 General Price List Study (released December 8, 2023), but your own cost depends on the funeral home and the choices you make. Under the FTC Funeral Rule, you can ask a funeral home for prices by phone, get a General Price List to keep, and buy only the goods and services you want. Many families don't have that money set aside, and the bill falls on a spouse or adult children, sometimes paid with credit cards or loans.

A small, permanent whole life policy can solve this. You pick a face amount close to the costs you expect to leave. On a whole life final expense policy the premium is usually set at the start and stays level; check the policy to confirm. The coverage does not end after a set term the way term life does. Under the IRS's rules, a beneficiary generally does not owe income tax on life insurance paid because of the insured's death, but interest added to the payment is taxable. The insurer pays after it receives proof of death and the claim form.
replacements.why: Plan item 5: removes "usually $10,000 to $25,000", "Premiums never change", "typically within a couple of weeks", the unsourced "several thousand dollars and often into five figures" and "hardship withdrawals / quick-sold belongings". Adds the IRS source for tax treatment (with the interest exception), the FTC Funeral Rule link and rights, and the dated NFDA 2023 study link. NFDA dollar medians are not restated because the owner rule allows dollar amounts only from a primary government source (NFDA is a trade association). Checker: confirmed IRS (interest exception), FTC rights (prices by phone, a General Price List to keep, buy only what you want) and the NFDA release date; proof-of-death line backed by the Virginia guide.

replacements.new: Insurers sort final expense applicants into underwriting classes. The names and rules differ by insurer, but these four types are common. The class you land in can change your premium a great deal for the same face amount, so know which one you are in.

replacements.old: Best rate, day-one full coverage. For applicants in good health — no major medical events in the past 24 months, no recent cancer treatment, no insulin-dependent diabetes, no heart attack or stroke history. Most healthy 55- to 75-year-olds qualify.
replacements.new: Lower rate, full coverage from the first day. For applicants whose answers to the insurer's health questions raise no concerns. Each insurer writes its own questions and look-back periods, so the same health history can land in different classes at different companies.
replacements.why: Plan item 5: removes the generic underwriting rules ("no major medical events in the past 24 months...", "Most healthy 55- to 75-year-olds qualify") and the superlative "Best rate".

replacements.old: Mid-tier rate, day-one full coverage. For applicants with some health concerns — controlled diabetes, treated cancer history with appropriate wait periods, controlled high blood pressure. Premiums run meaningfully higher than Preferred.
replacements.new: Mid-tier rate, full coverage from the first day. For applicants with some health conditions that an insurer still accepts for the full benefit. Which conditions qualify depends on the insurer. Premiums are higher than Preferred.

replacements.old:
What is final expense insurance?
Final expense is a small whole life policy — usually $10,000 to $25,000 in face amount — designed to cover funeral, burial, and other end-of-life costs. Premiums are level and never change, the coverage doesn't expire, and the death benefit pays out tax-free, typically within a couple of weeks of a filed claim.
What's the first question to ask a final expense agent?
Ask which underwriting class you're being placed in: Preferred, Standard, Graded Benefit, or Guaranteed Issue. The class can change your premium by 50% or more for the same face amount. A common bad-faith move is selling Guaranteed Issue to people who could qualify for Preferred or Standard just because the application is easier.
What is the nonforfeiture trap?
Many whole life policies default the nonforfeiture option to Extended Term Insurance, which converts your cash value into term coverage that eventually expires — defeating the point of permanent insurance. For most final expense buyers, Reduced Paid-Up Insurance is the better choice and should be set during the application.
replacements.new:
What is final expense insurance?
Final expense insurance is a small whole life policy meant to cover funeral, burial or cremation costs and final bills. You choose the face amount. On a whole life final expense policy the premium is usually level, and the coverage lasts for life as long as you pay. Under IRS rules the death benefit is generally not taxable income to your beneficiary; interest paid on it is taxable. Graded and guaranteed-issue policies may pay only a reduced amount, such as the premiums paid, if death comes in the early years, often the first 2 or 3; the exact period is in the policy.
What's the first question to ask a final expense agent?
Ask which underwriting class you're being placed in: Preferred, Standard, Graded Benefit, or Guaranteed Issue (names vary by insurer). The class can change your premium a great deal for the same face amount, and the graded and guaranteed-issue classes limit what your family receives in the early years. A bad-faith move is selling Guaranteed Issue to people who could qualify for Preferred or Standard just because the application is easier.
What is the nonforfeiture trap?
If you stop paying, the policy uses the nonforfeiture option you chose, or its default if you didn't choose one. On some policies the default is Extended Term Insurance, which turns your cash value into term coverage that ends after a set time. Reduced Paid-Up Insurance keeps a smaller benefit for life, with no more premiums due. Ask which option your policy uses and whether you can choose Reduced Paid-Up on the application.
